problem: tracking make-up work for absent students
intro: To manage make-up work for absent students, keep one log, reuse the original post, and send one standard message. Start with the log, because every other step depends on it. This page covers the routine, the Google Classroom and Gmail steps on Mac, and where Lazur fits in.
tldr: Keep one make-up log with a row for every missed item and a date.
In Google Classroom, use Classwork > Create > Reuse post instead of retyping instructions.
Send one standard message from Gmail, then check the log against Classroom every week.
No study measures make-up work directly, so treat these steps as a routine to test in your own classes.

blocks.text: What the evidence says about make-up work for absent students

A search turned up no study that measures how long make-up work takes or how often it gets done. The evidence here is indirect. It covers attendance, achievement, and general teacher workload. Read it as context for your routine, not as proof that one system works.

Absence is common. Attendance Works reports at least 14.7 million students were chronically absent in the 2020-21 school year, roughly double the pre-COVID figure of more than 8 million. EdWeek puts national chronic absence near 22% in 2024-25. In that year, roughly half of urban districts had more than 30% of students chronically absent.
Why absence hurts the whole class

One study looked at about 23,000 students in grades 3 and 4 in a large East Coast urban district. Students in classrooms with no chronically absent peers had test scores about 10% higher on average. Students in classrooms where half were chronically absent scored lower. The study is correlational, so it cannot prove cause.

The author suggests teachers may slow instruction to help absent students catch up, and that disruption takes class time. That is a good reason to get make-up work to students fast. A student who waits a week for a packet is a student the class has already moved past.

The kindergarten picture points the same way. Gottfried and Ansari used national data on 18,170 kindergarteners in a 2022 study. Higher classroom percent absent went with lower reading scores, 38.28 points lower in their models, and lower math scores, 39.47 points lower. That study measured classroom absence, not chronic absence, so treat it as a signal.
How much teacher time is already spoken for

Make-up work competes with everything else in your week. A 2022 EdWeek survey, attributed to the EdWeek Research Center for Merrimack College, reported a median of 54 hours worked per week. Teachers in that survey reported about 5 hours on grading and feedback. They reported about 3 hours on general administrative work.

Those are general workload numbers. None of them isolates make-up work. They still show how little slack most weeks have. OECD survey data, reported by EdWeek in October 2025, found US lower-secondary teachers worked more than 45 hours a week in 2024. That was nearly five hours above the OECD average. A loose make-up process costs more time than it looks like on any single day.
A worked example of tracking missed assignments for absent students

Take a student who misses Monday through Wednesday. In that time the class covers two lessons, one worksheet, and a short quiz. On Thursday the student returns and asks what they missed. If you answer from memory, the quiz is the item most likely to slip through.

Now run the same case with a routine. On Monday afternoon, add a row for each missed item to the make-up log. Each row has the absence date, the item, and the Classroom post it belongs to. On Thursday morning, send one message with the list and a due date. Nobody has to remember anything from Monday.

items: Log each missed item the day you see the absence, not later.
Find the original Classroom post or attachment for each item.
Reuse the post for the student, or send the attachment by Gmail.
Set a due date, write it in the log, and include it in the message.
Check the log on the due date and mark each item returned, late, or excused.

blocks.text: The example works because the log holds the details. You still decide whether a missed quiz gets a retake, a different version, or no credit. Make that decision once, write it in your policy, and apply it the same way to every student.
Build a make-up log you can keep up with

A make-up log is one table with one row per missed item. You do not need a special app for it. A Google Doc or a Pages table works. Keep it in a place your school allows for student records, and keep one log per class.

rows: Starts the clock on the due date
Date and method you sent the work
Date the work is due back
Gives you one date to check
blocks.caption: The five columns of a make-up log, one row each.

blocks.text: Five columns cover most cases. Add a sixth only if your school requires something you must track. Use initials or student IDs if your school prefers them. Names make the log easier to read, and they also make it sensitive. Check your district's rules before you put names in any document.
Reuse the original post in Google Classroom for absent students

Google Classroom can copy a post for the student who missed it. On a computer, go to Classwork > Create > Reuse post. Select the original post. Check Create new copies of all attachments if the student needs their own files. Click Reuse, then choose Assign, Ask, or Post, or save a draft.

Attachments do not copy by default. The reused post links to the same files, so an edit to the original shows up in the copy too. That helps when you fix a worksheet once. It hurts when you want a frozen version for one student, so check the box if you need separate copies.

Assigning to individual students has two catches. If the original post went to individual students, the reused post defaults to all students. Check the student list before you click Assign. You also cannot assign to individual students across multiple classes, so reuse the post once in each class.
Send the make-up message in Gmail without retyping it

Most make-up messages say the same things. They list the missed lessons, where the work is, and when it is due. Write that message once. Change two or three fields for each student. Keep the template in Gmail drafts, or in a Pages or Google Doc you copy from.

Dictation helps with the repeated parts. Hold fn and speak, and Lazur dictates clean text at your cursor in any app. Snippets can store the standard paragraph, so you can insert it by name. Keep student names out of your personal dictionary, because that content is student data.

For the send itself, Gmail works like any compose window. Put the family or student address in To. Check CC and BCC before you send, especially if a counselor or administrator needs a copy. There is a short guide to these fields in [CC and BCC in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/add-cc-and-bcc-in-gmail).
Set a repeating reminder for the weekly log check

A weekly check keeps the log honest. Apple Reminders can repeat a reminder, so the check comes back without you planning it. The steps are short. Open the reminder's details, turn on Date, then open the pop-up menu next to Repeat and choose a schedule.

items: Create a reminder called Check make-up log.
Open the reminder's details and turn on Date.
Open the pop-up menu next to Repeat and choose a weekly schedule.
Set End Repeat if the check should stop on a set date, such as the end of a grading period.

blocks.text: Lazur can add a Reminders item by voice, so you can say it while you walk to class. Check the repeat schedule afterward, because Repeat is a separate step. Ask Lazur to guide you through it if the menu looks different on your Mac.
Decide the make-up policy before the absence happens

Many make-up fights start because the rule lived in one teacher's head. Write a short policy and share it early in the term. It should say how long a student has to return work, whether late work earns full credit, and what happens to missed quizzes. One page is enough.

Set the policy with your department where you can. A shared rule protects you when a family asks why one student got more time and another did not. It also gives you one answer when a student asks on the last day of the week.

blocks.title: Excused is not the same as zero
blocks.text: Do not record an excused absence as a missed grade until you check your school's rule. Schools handle excused work differently, so ask your administrator before you change a grade.
Edge cases that break a simple make-up routine

items: A student misses a unit test, not just a daily lesson.
A student is out for a week while the class moves on to a new unit.
A student is excused for one day but still owes a long assignment.
A student returns with work done at home but no clear date on it.
A group project loses a member who still needs a role.

blocks.text: For a missed unit test, pick one option and write it in the log: a retake, a different version, or a reweighted grade. Use the same option for every student who misses it. For a long absence, talk to the counselor or family before you send a packet. A week of work may need a plan, not a stack of photocopies.

Chronic absence is a different problem from a single missed week. If a student misses school often, the make-up list is one piece of the answer. Families need to hear from you early, and the support team should know what is still open.
Mistakes teachers make with make-up assignments

items: Keeping the list in your head, then missing the student who asked only once.
Sending the full class packet to a student who missed two items.
Assigning in Classroom without checking the individual student list.
Editing a shared attachment after some students already downloaded it.
Changing the policy for each family instead of writing one rule.
Pasting student names into an AI tool without checking your district's rules.

blocks.text: Most of these come from one habit. The routine lives in your memory rather than in a record. Fix the record first, and the rest gets easier to handle.
Privacy and student records when you use AI tools

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold ⌥⌘. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. A screenshot of a roster or a log can still show student names, so check your district's rules first.

A safe habit is simple. Close the roster, or use initials, before you hold ⌥⌘. Ask about the menu or the step, not about one student's record. Research in Lazur runs in its own Chrome tabs. Use it for public pages, such as a published district policy, and keep student records out of it.
Where Lazur helps with this routine, and where it does not

Lazur guides, points, explains, drafts, and dictates. Ask where the Reuse post option sits, and Lazur circles the label on your screen. Ask how to set a reminder, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. It does not click buttons or edit your Classroom for you.

Lazur is not a gradebook. It does not track which student owes what, and it is not a plugin for Classroom or Gmail. Your log and your Classroom stay the record. Lazur helps you find the right menu, write the message, and set the reminder faster.
Your next steps after the first week

After the first week, count how many items came back on time. Count them in the log, not from memory. If the same day or class keeps producing gaps, the problem is the absence pattern, not the paperwork. Bring that pattern to your counselor or family, and adjust the routine where it breaks.

faq.question: How do I reuse a Google Classroom post for a student who was absent?
faq.answer: On a computer, go to Classwork > Create > Reuse post. Select the original post, choose whether to copy attachments, then click Reuse. Pick Assign, Ask, or Post, or save a draft. Check the student list before you assign.

faq.question: Do attachments copy when I reuse a post in Google Classroom?
faq.answer: Not by default. The reused post links to the same attachments, so edits to the original file show up in the copy. Check Create new copies of all attachments if the student needs their own copy.

faq.question: Can I assign reused work to one student instead of the whole class?
faq.answer: Yes, within one class. If the original post went to individual students, the reused post defaults to all students, so select the individual students again. You cannot assign to individual students across multiple classes.

faq.question: How do I set a repeating reminder on Mac?
faq.answer: Open the reminder's details in Apple Reminders and turn on Date. Then open the pop-up menu next to Repeat and choose a schedule. Use End Repeat if the reminder should stop on a set date.

faq.question: Should a student lose points for missed work?
faq.answer: That depends on your school's policy. Write the rule once, share it, and apply it the same way to every student. Treat excused absences separately, and check your school's rule before you change a grade.

faq.question: Does Lazur see my student list or gradebook?
faq.answer: Lazur looks at your screen only while you hold ⌥⌘. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. If student names are on screen, close the roster or use initials first.

faq.question: Is there research proving that a make-up log improves grades?
faq.answer: No study found in this review measures make-up logs directly. The research covers attendance and achievement in general. Treat the routine as a practical habit to test in your own classes, not as a proven method.

faq.question: Does Lazur sync with Google Classroom or track assignments for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it does not operate other apps for you. It points, guides, drafts, and dictates. Your gradebook and Classroom remain the record.

costs.title: Hours lost each week
costs.text: Teachers already work a median 54 hours a week, according to a 2022 EdWeek survey. Answering the same make-up questions by email or at the door uses time that could go to grading and planning. The cost comes back every week, so small delays add up.

costs.title: Grades that measure logistics
costs.text: A student who never saw the quiz can get a low score for a reason unrelated to learning. Grades then reflect who was in the room that day, not what the student knows. That creates a grading problem you have to fix by hand later.

costs.title: Students who fall behind the class
costs.text: Gottfried's study linked classrooms with more chronically absent peers to lower test scores on average. The author suggests teachers may slow instruction to help absent students catch up. Untracked missed work widens the gap for the student who was out.

costs.title: Family disputes over fairness
costs.text: A family that does not know what was missed, or when it is due, can see the teacher as unfair. Clear written dates and one standard message help prevent most of these arguments. Without them, every case becomes a new conversation.

causes.title: Absence arrives in small pieces
causes.text: A student misses one lesson on Monday, one quiz on Tuesday, and a worksheet on Wednesday. No single item feels urgent, so none gets logged. By Friday the gaps add up, and nobody can say exactly what the student owes.

causes.title: Work lives in too many places
causes.text: Handouts sit in Google Docs, instructions sit in Classroom, and slides sit in Keynote or Pages. A student who was out may need all three. Searching across apps takes time, and sending the wrong file is easy to do.

causes.title: The record sits in your head
causes.text: Teachers track make-up work from memory, sticky notes, and the last email thread. Memory works for one student and fails for six. The week you are busiest is usually the week the list falls apart.

causes.title: No written policy
causes.text: If the rule is unwritten, every case becomes a negotiation. Families ask why one student got more time. You end up deciding each case from scratch, which takes time and invites complaints from others.

causes.title: Chronic absence is widespread
causes.text: Attendance Works reported at least 14.7 million chronically absent students in the 2020-21 school year. At that scale, make-up work is a steady load, not an occasional one. A system built for rare cases breaks under that volume.

causes.title: Repeat absences hide patterns
causes.text: A student who misses every Monday has a pattern. A log that tracks only individual items does not show it. Without a pattern view, the same gaps return, and you treat each one as new.

fixes.title: Start one make-up log today
fixes.text: Make one table with the five columns from this page. Use one log per class. Add a row on the day a student is absent. A row takes less time to fill in than a list rebuilt from memory later.

fixes.title: Reuse the original Classroom post
fixes.text: Use Classwork > Create > Reuse post instead of retyping instructions. Check the student list before you assign, because the default can be all students. Reuse the post once in each class where you need it.

fixes.title: Write a one-page make-up policy
fixes.text: Put the due window, the credit rule, and the quiz rule on one page. Share it at the start of the term and post it in each Classroom class. Students then see the rule where they already look for work.

fixes.title: Use one standard message
fixes.text: Keep one message that lists the missing items and the due date. Change the student or family name and the dates for each case. Save the paragraph as a Lazur snippet if you dictate it often.

fixes.title: Set a weekly reminder for the log check
fixes.text: Create a reminder with Repeat set to weekly. The check takes only a few minutes. The reminder keeps the check from slipping during the busiest weeks of the term.

fixes.title: Ask families what gets in the way
fixes.text: A 2023 Learning Heroes and TNTP study found that schools with stronger family engagement had chronic absence rates about 6 percentage points lower after remote learning. EdWeek reports districts often find fixable problems, such as unclear bus routes. Send a short note asking what gets in the way.

fixes.title: Dictate the repeated notes
fixes.text: Hold fn to dictate a note in any app. Use snippets for lines you type every week. Keep student names out of the personal dictionary, because the dictionary is a place where that content can end up.

fixes.title: Check the log against Classroom before the due date
fixes.text: Compare the Status column with what Classroom shows before the due date. Catch missing items early, while the student can still complete them. A late catch is harder to fix than an early one.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Set up the make-up log
plan.text: Create one table with five columns: absence date, item missed, sent, due, and status. Make one log for each class. Store it where your district allows student records. Add a row for every open item already on your list.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Write the one-page policy
plan.text: Write the due window, the credit rule, and the quiz rule in plain words. Ask a department colleague to read it. Post it in each Classroom class so the rule sits where students already look.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Log absences before first period
plan.text: Check attendance and add a row for each missed item. Find the matching Classroom post so the packet is ready before lunch. Keep the check short, and do it the same way every day.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Send one standard message
plan.text: Open the template in Gmail drafts. Change the name, the dates, and the missing items. Check CC and BCC, then send. Write the sent date in the Sent column the same day.

plan.label: Weekly
plan.title: Check the log against Classroom
plan.text: Use a repeating Reminders item to check the log every week. Compare the Status column with what Classroom shows. Chase open items while the due date is still ahead of you.

plan.label: Week 2
plan.title: Change one thing at a time
plan.text: Fix one source of friction, such as a missing due date or an unclear credit rule. Leave the rest alone. Changing everything at once makes it hard to tell what helped.
